HISTORY AND PHYSICAL (H&P) NOTE  

History:  
• 19-year-old female presents with dysuria, urinary frequency, and suprapubic discomfort for “just under a week” (initially said 3 days – conflict noted).  
• Reports stinging/burning on micturition and pink-tinged urine observed today.  
• Suprapubic aching pain, worst while voiding; does not radiate to flanks or back.  
• Denies nausea, vomiting, fever, flank pain, or new bowel changes.  
• No abnormal vaginal discharge.  
• Sexually active with long-term boyfriend; uses combined oral contraceptive pill; last unprotected intercourse ≈1 week ago. Last menstrual period 2 weeks ago; no pregnancy concerns raised by patient.  
• Tried cannabis once 1½ weeks ago; occasional social alcohol use; non-smoker otherwise.  

Past Medical History:  
• Irritable bowel syndrome.  
• No known kidney or bladder disease.  

Allergies:  
• Clindamycin – adverse reaction (“didn’t go too well”).  

Medications:  
• Combined oral contraceptive pill – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Mebeverine (antispasmodic for IBS) – dose/route/frequency not documented.  

Physical Examination:  
(Consult conducted via telehealth; no formal exam performed)  
• Patient appears well, alert, conversational.  
• No reported fever, back/flank pain, or systemic symptoms.  

Impression:  
Acute uncomplicated cystitis (urinary tract infection).  

Management Plan:  
• Empiric oral antibiotic: Nitrofurantoin 3-day course OR Trimethoprim (choice discussed).  
• Obtain mid-stream urine sample today for dipstick and culture; patient to drop sample at clinic.  
• Advise increased oral fluids.  
• Analgesia: Paracetamol as needed.  
• Safety-net: seek care urgently for fever, worsening pain, flank/back pain, or vomiting.  
• Routine follow-up if no improvement within 1 week or recurrence of symptoms.  

Patient Summary:  
19-year-old university student with 1-week history of dysuria, frequency, mild hematuria, and suprapubic ache—most consistent with uncomplicated UTI. Empiric antibiotics started and urine culture arranged; warned about red-flag symptoms and follow-up.  

Key Takeaways:  
1. Start prescribed 3-day antibiotic course immediately and complete it.  
2. Drink plenty of water; take paracetamol for discomfort.  
3. If fever, back pain, vomiting, or no improvement in a week, contact the clinic or seek urgent care.  

Next Steps:  
• Submit urine sample today; clinic will relay culture results and adjust antibiotics if needed.  
• Return for review or repeat testing if symptoms persist/worsen.  
• Consider pregnancy test if menses delayed or symptoms atypical.  

Quality checks (document_quality):  
• Missing expected elements: vitals, abdominal/pelvic exam findings, pregnancy test, detailed antibiotic prescription (drug/dose/route/frequency).  
• Internal conflict: symptom duration stated as 3 days vs “just under a week.”  
• Transcript quality: clear; minimal background noise; no major inaudible sections.
